title: Behar: hold him before he falls (Leviticus 25:35)
hookLine: support a struggling neighbor before he falls; Maimonides calls this the highest giving

cards: A donkey on a dirt road with a heavy sack on its back. The sack starts to slip. One person walking alongside can put a hand on it and push it back into place.
Easy. Now let it fall. It's in the dust, split open, grain everywhere, and even five people together can't heave it back up.
The picture comes from an old rabbinic commentary on a single verse in this week's portion. It isn't about donkeys. It's about the moment a neighbor's life starts to slip.

teach.b: Leviticus twenty-five, verse thirty-five, still in Behar. If your brother grows poor and his means begin to fail beside you, "then thou shalt uphold him". In Hebrew, v'hechezakta bo: take hold of him, strengthen him.
The ancient commentary called the Sifra, and Rashi after it, read the verb with care. It doesn't say lift him up off the ground.
It says hold him, which only works while he's still standing. That's where the donkey comes from: catch the load while it's slipping, because once it's down, it takes a crowd.
Moses Maimonides wrote out eight levels of giving to the poor, from the one who gives grudgingly at the bottom to the very top. And the top rung isn't the biggest donation, or even the anonymous one.
It's this verse: strengthen someone before they need to ask, with a gift, a loan, a partnership, or finding them work, so they can stand on their own. He quotes thou shalt uphold him as the proof.
So the highest form of charity isn't a rescue. It's prevention. It happens quietly, before anyone has to stand in a line or fill out a form or say the hard words, I need help.
It keeps a person's dignity whole, and keeps them a neighbor instead of a case.
The verse goes on: let him live with thee. Not beneath you. With you.

how: Jewish communities run free-loan societies, job networks and quiet support funds often linked to this verse; Maimonides' eight levels of giving, from the Mishneh Torah's laws of gifts to the poor, are widely taught, with helping someone become self-supporting at the top.

games.q: holding a neighbor up — tap the pairs.

s: for Maimonides, the highest giving is the largest gift
the top rung is strengthening someone so they don't need to ask: a loan, a partnership, a job.
the commentary compares a struggling neighbor to a slipping load
hold it while it slips; once it falls, it takes many hands.
the verse says the poor neighbor should live beneath you
it says let him live with thee.

games.q: a friend's business is wobbling. they haven't asked for anything. what does Maimonides put at the top of the ladder of giving?
o: wait until they ask, then give generously.
help now, with a loan, partnership or work, so they stay standing.
games.why: the highest level, in Gifts to the Poor 10:7, is strengthening someone before they fall, so they never need to ask. he cites "thou shalt uphold him."

practice: Let faces come to mind: a friend who's gone quiet, a coworker whose hours were cut, a relative carrying more than they say. Notice whose load seems to be slipping.
Then think of one small way to put a hand on the sack, an introduction, a ride, a meal, a lead on a job, a message that says I noticed, and hold that person in mind for a while.

wordCard.voice: Behar, the portion on the mountain. One of its teachings: strengthen a neighbor while they're still standing. The next portion begins tomorrow.

orig.note: Hebrew: and you shall uphold him. from chazak, strong: strengthen him.

carryVoice: Your line: hold him before he falls. One hand, early, does what five can't do later. That's four hundred twenty-four days.
